Geumhomun Gate is currently the temporary entrance to Changdeokgung Palace. The original main gate was Donhwamun, but due to Donhwamun repair work, you must now use Geumhomun.

When you arrive at Geumhomun, our staff will help you with directions and check your admission ticket or eligibility. The procedures are clearly outlined so you don't have to worry about getting lost. Geumhomun Gate is not the entrance with the most visitors, but the surrounding area is relatively quiet, so you can leisurely explore Changdeokgung Palace.

If you are planning to visit Changdeokgung Palace, please check the entrance change information before visiting and follow the on-site guidance signs. The entrance change will not have a significant impact on your visiting experience.

reviews.author: Choi Pan-dong
reviews.text: The royal library located in the Naegaksa area of Changdeokgung Palace. It was established after King Jeongjo ascended the throne. It is said that Gyujanggak was originally installed temporarily during the reign of King Sejo, but was soon abolished. Initially, Juhamnu Pavilion was built in the back garden of Changdeokgung Palace and Gyujanggak was placed there, but as it gradually became larger, it was moved here and Oegyujanggak was placed on Ganghwado Island. It was a place where numerous books and relics were stored, and later it also hosted civil service exams and the Chogyemun exam system. During the Japanese colonial period, it was transferred to Gyeongseong Imperial University, and after liberation, it was moved to the Seoul National University library, where it is still stored to this day.

reviews.author: Macoya Lee
reviews.text: Kyujanggak is a royal library first established in the year of King Jeongjo's accession to the throne. It is a palace institution that stores the writings of past kings and performs tasks such as compiling, printing, and distributing books. Currently, there are two places called Gyujanggak in Changdeokgung Palace. One is Gyujanggak, which is located on the lower level of Juhamnu in the back garden, and the other is this building in the area of ​​Gwolnaegaksa. It is unknown when Kyujanggak was first used, but it is said that Kyujanggak stored over 30,000 books, so it may have been used as a storage place.

reviews.author: BH Park
reviews.text:
If you pass through Donhwamun and go straight, you will come to Gwolnaegaksa Temple. If you turn left from here, the building you will see is Gyujanggak. On the right is the Prosecutor's Office.
Gyujanggak was originally built by King Jeongjo in 1776 on the Buyongji side of the rear garden of Changdeokgung Palace and served as a royal library to store the royal books. Currently, this building in Buyongji is called Juhamnu and can only be accessed by passing through Eosumun. Anyway, it is said that Gyujanggak, which was located in Buyongji, was moved to the current inside of Gwolnaegaksa in 1781.

King Sejo first established it to replace Jiphyeonjeon, and King Seongjong reorganized it into an academic institution. It was later destroyed during the Japanese invasions of Korea, but was rebuilt during the reign of King Gwanghaegun. It was demolished during the Japanese colonial rule and was restored in the 2000s to its current state. The current signboard was also made at that time, and it says ‘Okdang’ instead of Hongmungwan. Munjeongjeon, where Crown Prince Sado’s resentment is buried. It was in this front yard that I was trapped in the back gate, but it was not well known, so even though it was the weekend, it was quiet except for foreigners listening to the commentary. Although it is adjacent to Myeongjeongjeon, which is crowded with visitors, it feels more isolated because it is surrounded by a wall. As it is a restored area, I wondered what it would have been like if the back pillars had been left in place.

It is said that it was used as a wedding hall in the late Joseon Dynasty and was used as a wedding hall to hold the royal spirit. Although it does not exist now, it is said that in the past, there was a hallway for spirits installed in front of the pavilion.

It is said that the tragedy of Crown Prince Sado is also related to the fact that it was used as a wedding match. The memorial tablet of Queen Jeongseong, King Yeongjo's queen, was enshrined here, and there is a record that King Yeongjo said that her spirit appeared and warned the crown prince that he would cause an uprising. The prelude to the Imo Incident was announced under the pretext of Queen Jeongseong, and seeing that Crown Prince Sado was close to Queen Jeongseong during her lifetime brings many thoughts to mind.

reviews.author: Productive Minho
reviews.text:
Binyangmun Gate means “respectfully greeting the brightness.” Along with Myeongjeongjeon, which is the only Jeongjeon of the Joseon Dynasty that is placed toward the rising sun, the back gate, Binyangmun, also faces east. The naming is quite intuitive when you picture the kings who would walk from Naejeon, pass through Binyangmun, and go to Myeongjeongjeon on a sunny morning.

It is the back gate of Jeongjeon and connects Myeongjeongjeon, a public office area, and Naejeon, a daily living space, so it is a place where many visitors pass through. The course that runs through Honghwamun - Myeongjeongjeon - Naejeon makes it easy to tour Changgyeonggung Palace.

The characteristic of Binyangmun Gate is that it has a ceiling, a type of corridor, and the roof connects to Myeongjeongjeon and Munjeongjeon. It was also adjacent to Sungmundang, so it felt like each pavilion was organically intertwined. It is said that Cheonrang is difficult to find in traditional hanoks other than Seonjeonjeon at Changdeokgung Palace and Taewonjeon at Gyeongbokgung Palace.

It is said that it was built for the king or crown prince to study. It was originally the Changgyeonggung Palace area, but it was incorporated into the Nakseonjae area when Nakseonjae was built in this area during the reign of King Heonjong. It is said to be the oldest building in the Nakseonjae area. A pavilion at Changgyeonggung Palace that King Yeongjo and King Jeongjo often visited. Although it is small in size, it is built on a three-tiered long stone platform, giving it its own majesty. Perhaps because it was an accessory facility that the king was looking for, the ceiling was very ornate.

It is said that Haminjeong was a place where national feasts and royal ceremonies were held. It is said that the front yard of the pavilion was large, so the king would gather his subjects and those who had passed the national civil service exam to meet with him, and sometimes he would also invite the people to listen to the voices of the people.

reviews.author: Macoya Lee
reviews.text: This pavilion building in Changgyeonggung Palace was originally the site of Inyangjeon, built during the reign of King Seongjong. When Inyangjeon Hall was destroyed during the Japanese invasions of Korea, it was built in its place during the reign of King Injo. The building was originally built by relocating Hamindang from Ingyeonggung Palace built by Gwanghaegun, but it was rebuilt after it burned down during the reign of King Sunjo.  Originally, there were walls on all sides and the space was occasionally used as a private space, but now it is open on all sides. Inside, there are plaques with five words representing the spring, summer, autumn and winter written on them in all directions.

reviews.author: Choi Pan-dong
reviews.text: This building was built during the reign of King Injo, was destroyed by fire during the reign of King Sunjo, and was rebuilt afterwards. It is said that the very meaning of ‘Hamin’ means to be immersed in the spirit. It is said that they met with Confucian students who passed the civil service examination, held contests, or held simple ceremonies. It is said that King Yeongjo decided to call officials and ordinary people during peacetime to hear about economic evils and problems. It is said that the inside of the pavilion is filled with water all over the place. Inside the pavilion, there are poems written all over the place. Each verse contains the meaning of spring, summer, fall, and winter.

reviews.author: BH Park

Haminjeong was not a building built when Changgyeonggung Palace was first built. It was originally the site of a building called Inyangjeon. When Inyangjeon was destroyed by fire during the Japanese invasions of Korea, King Injo built Haminjeong in its place in 1633. However, in 1830, the 30th year of King Sunjo's reign, Changgyeonggung Palace caught fire and was completely destroyed, but was rebuilt in 1833.
Haminjeong is said to be a place where subjects who passed the civil service examination were met.

reviews.author: Productive Minho
reviews.text:
A stone pagoda from the mid-to-late Goryeo Dynasty, now called the Changgyeonggung Five-story Stone Pagoda, as its original location is unknown. It appears that Japan moved it for exhibition purposes during the Japanese colonial period, but since no data remains, the only vague speculation remains is that it was moved from Chungcheong/Jeolla-do.

It is said that an attempt was made to relocate the stone structure symbolizing the temple to Bongeunsa Temple due to controversy over the use of a stone structure symbolizing the temple in the palace of the Joseon Dynasty, which was governed by a system that suppressed Buddhism and Confucianism, but was aborted. The story is that only the Cultural Heritage Administration's vague slogan, “Changgyeonggung Palace itself is history,” remains.

Despite all the stories, the stone pagoda itself was charming and pretty. It was in a good state of preservation and was unique because it was of an uncommon style. Still, I thought it would be good if I could somehow find my way back to my original place.

reviews.author: Productive Minho
reviews.text:
A palace where kings and crown princes who visited Changgyeonggung Palace stayed. It is said to be the place where King Jungjong received treatment from Dae Jang Geum, and there is a history in which Crown Prince Sohyeon, the successor to King Injo, died mysteriously here. It is said that it has been widely used as a mortuary since the late 1600s. It is said that the funerals of King Jeongjo, Heonjong, Cheoljong, and several queens were held here.

It is also the point where the great fire at Changgyeonggung Palace broke out in 1830. At the time of the environmental battle, Crown Prince Hyomyeong, the crown prince of King Sunjo and a promising figure in the late Joseon Dynasty, died suddenly and the funeral home was set up, but it is said to have caught fire for unknown reasons.

There are many pavilions related to King Yeongjo in Changgyeonggung Palace, and this was one of them. It is said that the order given to Crown Prince Sado to take charge of affairs on behalf of the monarch was an environmental war. Afterwards, it leads to catastrophe. In any case, the records related to environmental warfare are generally dark.

It is said that it also sometimes served as a birth office, a government office for the queen and crown princess to give birth.

Crown Prince Sado's wife, Hyegyeonggung Hong, resides here, and it is also the place where King Jeongjo was born. According to the story, before giving birth to King Jeongjo, Crown Prince Sado had a dream of a dragon and drew the dragon he saw in his dream on the wall, but it is not known anymore.

After a meal, they can have tea at the cafe inside the museum or look around and admire the various exhibitions held in the various exhibition halls here, making it a great tourist course. However, you will need to plan your schedule well as waiting in line in front of Gaeseong Dumpling Restaurant can be close to 30 to 1 hour.
For reference, from the perspective of those renting this Gyeongin Museum of Art, the first exhibition room, located in the innermost area, is the largest exhibition room as it shares the first and second floors, but unfortunately, many of the visitors, who are elderly or who stop by for a short time, often do not go up to the second floor after looking around the first floor, so the works displayed on the second floor may have far fewer visitors than the exhibits on the first floor, so in the case of group exhibitions, The joys and sorrows of each member are mixed. Visited April 24, 2025
I discovered the Bukchon Hanok Village experience center on the way down from an enjoyable walk in Bukchon. You can receive free explanations about Hanok, and there is also a rest area for travelers and a workshop. There are various programs you can choose from. The Bukchon Cultural Center Hanok is a registered cultural asset, a modern Hanok, purchased and renovated by the Seoul Housing and Urban Corporation, and is being used as a base for Bukchon experience and tourism education. The shelter is currently open and many people were using it today as well. Sitting on the veranda, the buildings and sky seen beyond the tile roof are colorful.

reviews.author: Noh Jin-tak
reviews.text: It was a rewarding time to see at a glance the history of the revision of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea and the changes made by groundbreaking rulings since the establishment of the Constitutional Court.

reviews.author: Sam Chou
reviews.text: The Constitutional Court of the Republic of Korea is the highest constitutional court of the Republic of Korea, established in 1988. It plays the role of protecting constitutional order and the basic rights of the people. The Constitutional Court, located in Seoul, is comprised of nine judges who are appointed on the recommendation of the President, the National Assembly, and the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and their term of office is six years. This ensures diversity and checks and balances in the composition of the judges. The main functions of the Constitutional Court include impeachment review of the president and high-ranking public officials, review of the dissolution of political parties, review of the constitutionality of laws, review of authority disputes between state agencies, and review of constitutional appeals. The Constitutional Court has played a pivotal role in Korea's democratization process, establishing the principles of independence of the judiciary and protection of the Constitution, including dismissing the impeachment motion against President Roh Moo-hyun in 2004 and ruling that the impeachment motion against President Park Geun-hye was legal in 2017, leading to President Park's dismissal. The Constitutional Court is not only a place where judicial procedures are conducted, but is also the guardian of the democratic system that checks the abuse of power by the executive and legislative branches and protects the freedom and rights of the people through independent judgment. The existence of the Constitutional Court symbolizes the maturity of Korea's constitutional system and the importance of its democratic oversight function.

Perhaps because it was a recently opened gallery, it was very clean and tidy. They also sell high quality coffee. The combination of high ceilings and white walls creates a comfortable space for viewing artwork. It may be a little difficult to find the entrance as it is located in the basement of the building, but once you enter, you will be amazed by the unexpected and unique atmosphere the works create.

Visited this gallery several times while in the area. A variety of works were on display, including sculptures, art toys, and abstract paintings. As it is a new gallery, it is still in the exploration stage, so the exhibition period was somewhat short, but I think it will get better in the future. Still, I was satisfied to see a variety of works.

I highly recommend this place.
